title: Hanukkah: the oil (Shabbat 21b)
hookLine: the Talmud's story of one jar of oil lasting eight days

cards: One little jar of oil, enough for one night, and it burned for eight. That's the Hanukkah of greeting cards and children's books, and it's why people eat foods fried in oil.

But yesterday's story, from First Maccabees, doesn't mention oil at all. The jar comes from a page of the Talmud, in the middle of a long discussion about which wicks and oils you may use for Shabbat candles.
And it starts with a question that sounds almost naive.

teach.b: The question, in tractate Shabbat, page 21b, is simply: what is Hanukkah? As if the rabbis are asking why keep it at all. The answer is a short story.
When the Greeks entered the Temple, they made all the oils impure.

teach.h: ONE JAR, THE HIGH PRIEST'S SEAL.
teach.b: When the Hasmonean family, the Maccabees, defeated them, they searched and found just one jar of oil still sealed with the high priest's seal.

teach.h: ONE DAY'S OIL, EIGHT DAYS' LIGHT.
teach.b: It held enough to light the lamp for a single day. A miracle happened, and they lit from it for eight days. The next year, the story ends, they set those days as festival days, for praise and thanksgiving.
That's the whole account: a few lines. Notice what it leaves out. No battles, no Judah, no Antiochus.
Readers explain this differently. Some suggest that after later revolts against Rome ended in disaster, the rabbis preferred to stress God's quiet help over victory in battle.
Others point out that the Talmud seems to assume its readers know the history, and only adds what's missing.
Either way, the story on the greeting cards is this one: not a war, but a lamp. And its point is small and stubborn. A sealed jar, one day's worth, nowhere near enough.
That's the miracle the rabbis chose to remember: not that there was plenty, but that the little they had was enough to begin.

how: Many Jews light Hanukkah lamps with olive oil to recall the jar in the Talmud's story, and eat foods fried in oil, like latkes and sufganiyot, during the eight nights.

o: the name of the lamp that stood in the Temple
a word meaning oil, from the jar that lasted
dedication, which the Talmud ties to a jar of oil

games.q: inside the Talmud's story — tap the pairs.

s: First Maccabees tells the story of the oil
First Maccabees tells of battles and a new altar; the jar of oil is the Talmud's telling.
in the Talmud's story, the jar was sealed with the high priest's seal
that seal showed the oil was still pure.
in the Talmud's story, the days were made a festival that same year
the next year, the story says, they set them as days of praise and thanksgiving.

games.q: you're a priest in the Temple. you've found one jar of pure oil, enough for a single day. making new pure oil will take days. what do you do?
o: mix it with the impure oil.
games.why: they lit it, and it burned for eight days. the rabbis remembered the lighting, not the waiting.

practice: Think of something you have only a little of right now: time, patience, energy, hope. Instead of waiting until there's enough, picture spending that little on purpose, like one kind word with the patience you have left.
Breathe slowly, as if you're watching a small flame hold.

wordCard.voice: Hanukkah. The dedication, and in the Talmud's telling, the eight days one jar of oil kept burning. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: a jar, or cruse, of oil, the small vessel at the center of the Talmud's story.

carryVoice: Your line: a little lasts. The jar was never enough, and they lit it anyway. See you tomorrow.
